title: 05 — Apache Iceberg Internals
html:
05 — Apache Iceberg Internals

The one idea: an Iceberg table is a tree of immutable files — a metadata file points to snapshots, each snapshot points to a manifest list, which points to manifests, which point to data files. A write builds a new branch of that tree off to the side and then swaps one pointer in the catalog. Readers always see a complete, consistent tree.

1. What Iceberg is (and is not)

Apache Iceberg is an open table format specification plus libraries (Java, Python, Rust, Go, C++) that implement it. It is not a database, not a query engine, and not a storage system. It specifies how to lay out metadata so that any engine can:

  • read a consistent snapshot of a table while it is being written,
  • commit changes atomically with optimistic concurrency,
  • prune files using statistics without listing directories,
  • evolve schema and partitioning without rewriting data,
  • time travel to earlier snapshots.

Format versions: v1 (analytic tables, append/overwrite), v2 (row-level deletes via delete files), v3 (deletion vectors, row lineage, default column values, variant, nanosecond timestamps, geospatial types). Check which version each engine you use supports before upgrading a table.

2. The metadata tree

---
title: Iceberg metadata tree
---
flowchart TD
    CAT["Catalog<br/>silver.nav -> v3.metadata.json"] --> MJ["Table metadata (v3.metadata.json)<br/>schemas, partition specs, sort orders,<br/>snapshots, refs (branches and tags)"]
    MJ --> S2["Snapshot S2<br/>(older)"]
    MJ --> S3["Snapshot S3<br/>(current)"]
    S3 --> ML["Manifest list<br/>snap-S3.avro"]
    S2 --> ML2["Manifest list<br/>snap-S2.avro"]
    ML --> M1["Manifest A<br/>partition 2026-09"]
    ML --> M2["Manifest B<br/>partition 2026-10"]
    ML2 --> M1
    M1 --> D1["data-001.parquet"]
    M1 --> D2["data-002.parquet"]
    M2 --> D3["data-003.parquet"]
    M2 --> DEL["delete file / deletion vector"]

Notice that S2 and S3 share manifest A. A new snapshot only writes manifests for what changed; everything else is reused. That is why commits are cheap and time travel is free.

2.1 Catalog entry

Holds one thing per table: the location of the current metadata file. The commit is a compare-and-swap on that location: "change it from v2 to v3 only if it is still v2".

2.2 Table metadata file (*.metadata.json)

{
  "format-version": 2,
  "table-uuid": "5d1c…",
  "location": "s3://warehouse/silver/nav",
  "last-sequence-number": 3,
  "current-schema-id": 1,
  "schemas": [ { "schema-id": 0, "fields": [ … ] }, { "schema-id": 1, "fields": [ … ] } ],
  "default-spec-id": 0,
  "partition-specs": [ { "spec-id": 0, "fields": [ { "source-id": 2, "field-id": 1000,
                         "name": "nav_date_month", "transform": "month" } ] } ],
  "current-snapshot-id": 7311,
  "snapshots": [
    { "snapshot-id": 6114, "timestamp-ms": 1761900000000, "manifest-list": "s3://…/snap-6114.avro",
      "summary": { "operation": "append", "added-records": "4210" } },
    { "snapshot-id": 7311, "parent-snapshot-id": 6114, "manifest-list": "s3://…/snap-7311.avro",
      "summary": { "operation": "overwrite", "deleted-records": "12", "added-records": "12" } }
  ],
  "refs": {
    "main":               { "snapshot-id": 7311, "type": "branch" },
    "vintage_2026_10_31": { "snapshot-id": 6114, "type": "tag" }
  },
  "metadata-log": [ { "metadata-file": "s3://…/00001-….metadata.json", "timestamp-ms": … } ]
}

Every version of the table's structure lives here: all schemas ever used, all partition specs, all snapshots still retained, and named refs.

2.3 Manifest list (snap-*.avro)

One per snapshot. One row per manifest, with the partition value ranges that manifest covers and counts of added/deleted files. A query on nav_date = 2026-10-31 skips every manifest whose month range excludes October without opening it.

2.4 Manifest files (*-m0.avro)

One row per data or delete file:

Field Purpose
file_path, file_format, record_count, file_size_in_bytes Locate and size the file
partition The partition tuple of this file
lower_bounds, upper_bounds, null_value_counts, value_counts per column ID File-level pruning
status ADDED / EXISTING / DELETED in this snapshot
content DATA, POSITION_DELETES or EQUALITY_DELETES

2.5 Data files and delete files

  • Data files: Parquet (or ORC/Avro) holding rows.
  • Position delete files (v2): "row 17 of file X is deleted".
  • Equality delete files (v2): "any row where isin = 'INE…' AND nav_date = … is deleted" — cheap for streaming writers, expensive for readers.
  • Deletion vectors (v3): a compact bitmap per data file stored in a Puffin file, replacing position delete files.

3. How a read works, step by step

  1. Engine asks the catalog for silver.nav → gets the current metadata location (and possibly temporary storage credentials).
  2. Reads the metadata JSON → picks the snapshot (current, or one chosen by time travel / ref).
  3. Reads that snapshot's manifest list → discards manifests whose partition ranges cannot match the filter.
  4. Reads the remaining manifests → discards data files whose column min/max cannot match.
  5. Reads only the surviving Parquet files → Parquet row-group statistics prune further.
  6. Applies any delete files / deletion vectors.

No directory listing happens at any point. That is the main reason Iceberg scales to millions of files.

4. How a write (commit) works, step by step

---
title: Iceberg optimistic commit
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Writer
    participant S as Object storage
    participant C as Catalog
    W->>C: load table (current = v2)
    W->>S: write new Parquet data files
    W->>S: write new manifest(s) for those files
    W->>S: write new manifest list (reuses unchanged manifests)
    W->>S: write v3.metadata.json (new snapshot, parent = current)
    W->>C: commit: swap v2 to v3 if still v2
    alt pointer still v2
        C-->>W: success, v3 is current
    else another writer committed first
        C-->>W: conflict
        W->>C: reload latest metadata
        W->>W: check the other commit does not conflict with mine
        W->>C: retry commit on top of the latest version
    end

Key properties:

  • Atomic: readers see either v2 or v3, never a mix.
  • Isolated: each reader is pinned to the snapshot it started with.
  • Optimistic concurrency: no locks; conflicts are detected at commit and retried. Appends to different partitions almost never conflict; two overwrites of the same partition do — one must fail or be re-planned.
  • Failed writes leave orphan files (written but never committed). They are invisible and are removed by orphan-file cleanup.

5. Snapshots, time travel, branches and tags

Every commit creates a snapshot: an immutable, complete version of the table.

Feature What it does Example use
Time travel by ID Read snapshot 6114 Reproduce a report exactly
Time travel by time Read the snapshot current at a timestamp "What did the table look like on 30 June 09:00?"
Tag A named, immutable pointer to a snapshot, with its own retention vintage_2026_10_31 = the certified month-end release
Branch A named, movable line of snapshots Write-audit-publish: write to staging branch, validate, then fast-forward main
Rollback Set main back to an earlier snapshot Undo a bad load in seconds 
-- Spark SQL examples
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav VERSION AS OF 6114;
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-06-30 09:00:00';
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav VERSION AS OF 'vintage_2026_10_31';     -- a tag

ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav CREATE TAG vintage_2026_10_31 RETAIN 3650 DAYS;
ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav CREATE BRANCH staging;
CALL lake.system.rollback_to_snapshot('silver.nav', 6114);
CALL lake.system.fast_forward('silver.nav', 'main', 'staging');

Time travel is system time — when the table changed. It is not the same as business history (when a fact was true in the world). For financial restatements you need both; see bitemporal modelling.

5.1 Write-audit-publish (WAP)

---
title: Write-audit-publish with branches
---
flowchart LR
    W["Write batch to branch 'staging'"] --> A["Audit: run quality checks<br/>against staging snapshot"]
    A -->|pass| P["Fast-forward main to staging"]
    A -->|fail| R["Leave main untouched<br/>quarantine batch"]

Consumers on main never see unvalidated data, and publishing is a metadata-only operation.

6. Hidden partitioning and partition evolution

In Hive-style tables, you add a nav_month column, populate it yourself, and every query must filter on nav_month or it scans everything. In Iceberg, the partition is a transform of an existing column, recorded in metadata:

Transform Example Result
identity(col) identity(source_id) The value itself
year/month/day/hour(ts) month(nav_date) 2026-10
bucket(N, col) bucket(16, isin) Hash into 16 buckets — spreads high-cardinality keys
truncate(W, col) truncate(4, isin) First 4 characters 
CREATE TABLE lake.silver.nav (isin string, nav_date date, nav decimal(18,4), scheme_code int)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (month(nav_date), bucket(8, isin));

-- Users just filter on the real column. Iceberg maps it to partitions.
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav WHERE nav_date BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-31';

Partition evolution: if daily volume grows, change the spec. Old files keep the old layout, new files use the new one, and the planner handles both. No rewrite.

ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav REPLACE PARTITION FIELD month(nav_date) WITH day(nav_date);

Partitioning guidance: aim for partitions holding at least hundreds of MB; do not partition by a high-cardinality column directly (use bucket); use sort order (WRITE ORDERED BY isin, nav_date) for clustering within partitions.

7. Schema evolution by field ID

Every column has a permanent field ID. Data files store IDs, not names. So:

Change Safe? Why
Add column Yes Old files have no such ID → read as null (or a v3 default)
Drop column Yes ID is ignored when reading
Rename column Yes Name is metadata; ID unchanged
Reorder columns Yes Position is metadata
Widen type (int → long, float → double, decimal(P,S) → decimal(P2,S) with P2 > P) Yes Readers up-cast
Narrow type, change string to int No Would need a rewrite 
ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav ADD COLUMN currency string AFTER nav;
ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav RENAME COLUMN nav TO nav_value;
ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav ALTER COLUMN scheme_code TYPE bigint;

8. Row-level changes: copy-on-write vs merge-on-read

Copy-on-write (COW) Merge-on-read (MOR)
On update/delete Rewrite every affected data file Write small delete files / deletion vectors
Write cost High Low
Read cost Low Higher until compacted
Best for Batch, read-heavy tables (Gold) Frequent small changes, CDC, streaming (Bronze/Silver) 
ALTER TABLE lake.silver.nav SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'merge-on-read'
);

MERGE INTO lake.silver.nav t
USING updates u
ON t.isin = u.isin AND t.nav_date = u.nav_date
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET nav_value = u.nav_value
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

9. Table maintenance

Without maintenance a busy table gets slow and expensive.

Job What it does Spark procedure
Compaction Combine small files, apply deletes, re-sort CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files('silver.nav', strategy => 'sort', sort_order => 'isin, nav_date')
Expire snapshots Remove old snapshots (and the files only they reference) CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots('silver.nav', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01', retain_last => 20)
Remove orphan files Delete files no snapshot references (failed writes) CALL lake.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'silver.nav')
Rewrite manifests Re-cluster manifests for faster planning CALL lake.system.rewrite_manifests('silver.nav')
Rewrite position deletes Compact delete files CALL lake.system.rewrite_position_delete_files('silver.nav')

Tagged snapshots are not expired while their tag retention lasts — which is how you keep certified vintages forever while expiring daily noise.

Useful table properties:

write.target-file-size-bytes   = 536870912      (512 MB)
write.parquet.compression-codec = zstd
history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms
history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep
write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled = true
write.metadata.previous-versions-max = 50

10. Metadata tables — inspecting a table with SQL

SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav.snapshots;      -- every snapshot, operation, summary
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav.history;        -- which snapshot was current when
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav.refs;           -- branches and tags
SELECT file_path, record_count, file_size_in_bytes FROM lake.silver.nav.files;
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav.manifests;
SELECT * FROM lake.silver.nav.partitions;     -- rows and files per partition: spot skew and small files

11. Questions to test yourself

  1. Draw the metadata tree from catalog to data file and say what each level lets a reader skip.
  2. Two writers append to different partitions at the same time. Does either fail? What if both overwrite the same partition?
  3. Why can Iceberg rename a column without rewriting data, when a Hive table cannot?
  4. What is the difference between a tag and a branch? Which would you use for a month-end certified release?
  5. A table has 400,000 files of 2 MB each. Which maintenance jobs do you run, in what order?
  6. Why is Iceberg time travel not enough to answer "what was revenue for FY24 as restated in 2026?"

12. Review checklist

  • Partition spec uses transforms; partitions hold hundreds of MB.
  • Sort order is set for the main filter columns.
  • COW or MOR chosen per table based on write pattern.
  • Compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan cleanup are scheduled.
  • Certified releases are tags with explicit retention.
  • Writes that need validation use a branch (write-audit-publish).
